query: How exactly should the Solomon 2x2 (pretest present/absent × treatment/control) be encoded in simr/powerlmm data generation and model formula syntax?

response.query: How exactly should the Solomon 2x2 (pretest present/absent × treatment/control) be encoded in simr/powerlmm data generation and model formula syntax?
response.answer: In simr/powerlmm, encode the Solomon 2x2 design with a model formula: y ~ treatment * pretest + (1 | subject). This includes interaction terms for treatment and pretest.

results.title: model theory - Arithmetization of Syntax: Can any semantic be encoded as syntax? - MathOverflow
results.content:
Title: model theory - Arithmetization of Syntax: Can any semantic be encoded as syntax? - MathOverflow
"According to model-theoretic interpretation, the semantics of a logical system describe whether a well-formed formula is satisfied by a given structure." - Wikipedia - Formal Systems. (1) The semantics of any logical system are able to be represented as syntax via the (orthodox) model-theoretic interpretation. (3) Semantics of a logical system which cannot be represented in the syntax of a logical system are merely stuff we haven't formalized yet (they aren't well-defined in the system). Gödel's Arithmetization of Syntax can only encode computably enumerable systems, so if you allow for systems of logic that are known to be non computaby enumerable, for example Second order logic with Full Semantics (For satisfiability to be representable by logical entailment you need the system to satisfy Gödel's Completeness theorem which fails for any attempted recursive axiomatization of SOL relative to full semantics), then there would be no way to reduce satisfiability to syntax. Now there are Philosophical positions that reject systems like SOL with full semantics from counting as a logical system (Quine's often quoted "Second order logic is Set theory in sheep's clothing" comes to mind). I will take point (2) to be referring to c.e logical systems in which case it is true under the caveat that semantics of a system is trivial unless you assume it's consistency, as there would be no models and the notion of satisfiability would be vacuous. Now for point (1) I take to mean that for any theory in some c.e. logical system U we can add new symbols to our syntax and rules describing a suitably strong foundational theory (like ZF + Con(U)) in which we can formalize the Model theory of that theory in the extended syntax. Point (3) seems to be referring to something like the full semantics problem mentioned earlier, and seems to be expressing the position that we can avoid it by replacing the true full semantics with an internal notion within the foundational theory (for SOL internally full models are ones were the second order domain is the powerset, in the sense of the model of ZF you are working in, of the first order domain) like what is presented in Jouko Väänänen Tracing Internal Categoricity.

results.title: Sage Research Methods - Encyclopedia of Survey Research Methods - Solomon Four-Group Design
results.content: #### All search filters on the page have been cleared. # Solomon Four-Group Design. The Solomon four-group design is an experimental design that assesses the plausibility of pretest sensitization effects, that is, whether the mere act of taking a pretest influences scores on subsequent administrations of the test. In the Solomon four-group design, the researcher randomly assigns respondents to one of four cells constructed from two fully crossed factors: treatment (e.g. treatment and control) and pretest administration (present or not). Richard Solomon first proposed a three-group design that consisted of an Experimental Group that was exposed to the pretest and the treatment; Control Group I that was exposed to the pretest, but not the treatment; and Control Group II that was not exposed to the pretest but received the treatment. Using this design, pretest sensitization is determined by conducting a two-factor analysis of variance (ANOVA), in which treatment and presence of pretest are the factors and posttest scores are the dependent variable.

results.content: Pretest-Posttest Design Study Guide | Quizlet ### Definition of Pretest-Posttest * A pretest is an assessment measure given to participants before they have undergone some type of treatment as part of a research study. * A pretest-posttest research design must provide participants with the same assessment measures before and after treatment in order to determine if any changes can be connected to the treatment. Types of Pretest-Posttest Design ### Randomized Control Group * Participants are randomly assigned to receive treatment, with non-treated participants forming the control group. * Both groups complete a pretest and a posttest to identify differences. Pros and Cons of Pretest-Posttest Design ### Randomized Control Group Design * Issues of validity arise, including internal and external validity. ### Solomon Four-Group Design * Absolves the weakness of external validity because it tests both pretested and un-pretested participants. Designing a Pretest-Posttest Experiment ### Process of Designing * Starts with a pretest administered to the participants, followed by the treatment, and then a posttest. ### Statistical Analysis * Analysis of pretest and posttest data needs to be completed by measuring the dependent variable before and after exposure to the treatment. results.title: Solomon Four-Group Design: An Introduction – QUANTIFYING HEALTH
results.content: # Solomon Four-Group Design: An Introduction. The **Solomon four-group design** is a type of experiment where participants get randomly assigned to either 1 of 4 groups that differ in whether the participants receive the treatment or not, and whether the outcome of interest is measured once or twice in each group. 1. A treatment group with both pre-intervention and post-intervention measurements (a.k.a. pretest and posttest). 2. A control group with both pretest and posttest measurements. 3. A treatment group with only a posttest measurement. 4. A control group with only a posttest measurement. Important notes regarding the Solomon four-group design:. 3. The design is asymmetric: Only participants in groups 1 and 2 receive pretest measurements (1A and 2A in the figure above), however, all participants receive posttest measurements (1B, 2B, 3B and 4B). ## Advantages of the Solomon four-group design. More specifically, what additional information can we get with a Solomon four-group design compared to a standard experimental design with 2 groups (1 treatment group and 1 control group)? ### How the Solomon four-group design resembles a two-group experimental design? Notice that the first 2 groups of this design resemble the pretest-posttest control group design. (For a detailed explanation, see my other article: Pretest-Posttest Control Group Design). The Solomon four-group design was developed to:. Something that a standard (two-group) experimental design can control. Something that a standard (two-group) experimental design cannot control. The general population from which participants were selected for the study will not be pretested, therefore, will not be sensitized to the intervention. #### How the Solomon four-group design helps detecting pretest sensitization? **Step #1:** Calculate the effect of the pretest on the outcome of the posttest in the presence of the intervention: This is the difference between 1B and 3B. ## Limitations of the Solomon four-group design. ## Example of a study that used the Solomon four-group design.
